name: SAM Shortline Excursion Train
dates: Selected weekends and holidays, March to December
customer: Families with kids, retired couples, train people
unique: Georgia's official rolling state park runs vintage coaches out of the 1888 Cordele depot across Lake Blackshear to Plains and Americus, with the car windows open and nobody in a hurry.
buzz: Riders talk about the lake crossing and the layover in Plains more than the seats. Book the dome car early for the summer runs.

name: Georgia Veterans State Park
customer: Families, anglers, golfers, veterans
unique: A state park built as a memorial to Georgia's war dead, with an outdoor museum of tanks and aircraft on the lawn, a Lake Blackshear beach, and a golf course cut through the pines.
buzz: The military museum on the grounds is the surprise. Locals come for the lake and the camping, and the collection gets a look on the way in.

name: Lake Blackshear
dates: Year round, warmest April to October
customer: Boaters, anglers, cypress photographers
unique: A flooded Flint River valley where dead cypress stand in open water, so you can idle a boat between gray trunks that died when the dam went in and never rotted.
buzz: The cypress water is the picture everyone takes. Fishing for crappie is the reason a lot of people keep a boat here.

name: Cordele Motor Speedway
customer: Short track fans, families, late model teams
unique: A paved half mile that hosts SpeedFest in January, when Super Late Model teams from across the Southeast shake down new cars in the cold.
buzz: SpeedFest is the draw, a January race weekend that pulls rigs from four states. The regular season is cheap, loud and easy to walk into.

name: Watermelon Days Festival
customer: Families, seed spitters, parade people
unique: The self-declared Watermelon Capital of the World throws a festival that is among the oldest in Georgia, with a parade, a 5K, a talent show and free slices cut on the courthouse lawn.
buzz: It is a genuine small town festival, not a craft fair with a theme. The seed spitting contest is the event people come back for.

name: Cordele State Farmers Market
dates: Year round, busiest May to August
customer: Road trippers, cooks, people buying a crate of peaches
unique: A state-run market shed where growers sell by the box, so you can buy a half bushel of peaches, a sack of pecans and a watermelon the size of a tire from the people who grew them.
buzz: In summer the sheds fill with melons and the smell carries. It is a working market, so go early and bring cash.

name: Sunbelt Ag Expo
customer: Farm families, equipment nerds, curious town people
unique: North America's largest outdoor farm show spreads over 100 acres of working plots, with combines cutting real corn, a tractor pull and every implement made for the southern row crop trade.
buzz: It is enormous and free parking, and the demo fields are the part outsiders do not expect. Bring boots, the grounds get deep.

name: Museum of Colquitt County History
customer: History people, genealogy visitors, grandparents with kids
unique: A volunteer county museum in the old courthouse annex with a room on the turpentine and naval stores camps that cleared this part of south Georgia, plus a wall of Moultrie-made rifles.
buzz: Small and county scale, and the turpentine room is the reason to stop. Hours are limited, so check before driving out.

name: The Arts Center of Moultrie
customer: Families, potters, people wanting a class
unique: A 1920s school converted into studios and galleries, with the Kaleidoscope children's museum inside and wheel throwing, painting and dance classes open to visitors.
buzz: The building itself is worth the walk, and the class list is longer than a town this size should manage. Call ahead for a drop-in spot.

name: Downtown Moultrie Murals
customer: Walkers, photographers, families
unique: A block by block run of wall murals around the 1902 courthouse square, including a full side of a building painted with the watermelon and cotton harvest this town was built on.
buzz: Easy hour on foot with coffee in reach. The square is intact enough that the murals read as part of the town rather than a decoration project.

name: Canopy of Lights
customer: Families, couples, anyone in town for the holidays
unique: The whole downtown grid is roofed in lights strung tree to tree, so the streets become a lit tunnel that switches on Thanksgiving night and runs into January.
buzz: People plan their drive home for it. The switch on night fills the square and is the closest this town gets to a crowd scene.

name: Doerun Pitcherplant Bog
dates: Year round, flowers April to June
customer: Botanists, birders, photographers, families
unique: Six hundred acres of longleaf pine and seepage bog where thousands of white-topped pitcher plants stand in the open, holding rainwater and whatever insects fell in.
buzz: The boardwalk makes it easy and the pitcher plants are dense enough to photograph without hunting. Best in spring when they flower, and the frogs are deafening.

name: Moss Farms Diving Facility
dates: Year round, outdoor season spring to fall
customer: Sports families, kids who want to try diving
unique: A farm pond outside Moultrie that became a national diving center with ten meter towers and eight springboards, and a record of sending divers to the Olympics that a small town should not be able to produce.
buzz: On a summer morning you can watch college and national team divers train for the price of a spectator fee. The beginner classes are the local kid rite of passage.

name: Georgia Museum of Agriculture and Historic Village
customer: Families, school groups, farm history people
unique: A recreated 1870s south Georgia town with a working steam train, a turpentine still, a grist mill and a farm, built as the state's agricultural museum and run by the college next door.
buzz: The train ride and the turpentine operation get the most talk. It is big enough to fill an afternoon and rarely crowded on weekdays.

name: Tift Theatre
customer: Touring acts, local audiences, families
unique: A 1935 Art Deco movie house on Main Street, restored and running again as a performing arts venue with a neon marquee that lights up the block.
buzz: The room is small enough that a touring country or tribute act feels close. Sightlines from the balcony are good and tickets stay cheap.

name: Rutland Farms Market and Corn Maze
customer: Families, pumpkin shoppers, school groups
unique: A working Tift County farm with a market of its own produce and a cut corn maze each fall, plus a u-pick strawberry field in spring.
buzz: The market is the steady draw, boiled peanuts and produce in season. The haunted maze nights in October sell out.

name: Downtown Tifton Historic District
customer: Walkers, shoppers, people off I-75
unique: A brick Main Street with a 1900s commercial block, the old Myon Hotel and a courthouse square, ten minutes off the interstate and far better than the exit ramp suggests.
buzz: It is a real downtown rather than a strip of antique shops. The coffee and the bakery on Main are why locals stop.

name: Coastal Plain Research Arboretum
customer: Gardeners, plant people, quiet walkers
unique: A university collection of native and adapted trees and shrubs laid out along a creek bottom, with labeled specimens of the longleaf, magnolia and cypress species that define this coastal plain.
buzz: Quiet, free and mostly empty. Gardeners use it as a reference collection, everyone else as a shady walk.

name: Andersonville National Historic Site
customer: History travellers, veterans, school groups
unique: The site of Camp Sumter, where nearly 13,000 Union prisoners died in fourteen months, and the only park in the system that memorialises every American prisoner of war, told inside the National Prisoner of War Museum.
buzz: People describe the museum as the part that stays with them, particularly the section on modern captivity. The reconstructed stockade and the cemetery take the rest of the visit.

name: Drummer Boy Civil War Museum
customer: Civil War collectors, history buffs
unique: A village storefront packed with original uniforms, a drum carried by a boy soldier, and Mary Surratt's bonnet, one of the few personal effects of a Lincoln conspirator on display anywhere.
buzz: Visitors call it a cabinet of real things rather than a storyboard museum. The Surratt bonnet is what they mention on the way out.

name: Pioneer Farm
customer: Families, history walkers
unique: A small farm compound behind the village with a working grist mill, a log cabin older than the Civil War and a blacksmith shop, laid out as a one-family Georgia farm of the 1850s.
buzz: It is quick and cheap and the mill still grinds. Good with kids after the national site, which is heavy going for them.

name: The Windsor Hotel
customer: Architecture people, couples, travellers stopping between Atlanta and Florida
unique: An 1892 railroad hotel with a five story atrium, a bridge across the light well and a staircase wide enough for hoop skirts, restored after decades of decline and still taking guests.
buzz: The atrium stops people in the door. Rooms are period sized, so ask for one of the larger corner ones and eat in the dining room at least once.

name: Rylander Theatre
customer: Touring acts, local audiences, theatre people
unique: A 1921 vaudeville and movie palace that sat dark for forty years and reopened in the 1990s, with a domed ceiling, gilt boxes and a schedule of touring music, theatre and film.
buzz: The restoration is the story locals tell. Sitting in the balcony for a show is the way to see the ceiling.

name: Georgia Rural Telephone Museum
customer: Phone nerds, families, roadside collectors
unique: One of the largest telephone collections in the country, in a small town exchange building, with switchboards, wooden wall phones, novelty handsets and a wall of colored sets from every decade.
buzz: Bigger than anyone expects for a town of 400. The switchboard room and the novelty phones are what people photograph.

name: Jimmy Carter National Historical Park
customer: History travellers, school groups, people who grew up with him
unique: Three sites in one small town, the depot that served as his campaign headquarters, the high school where the visitor center sits, and the farm without running water where he grew up, all preserved as they were.
buzz: Since his death the farm and depot draw steady crowds. The boyhood farm is the one people say made the man legible.

name: Cafe Campesino
customer: Coffee people, fair trade shoppers, remote workers
unique: Georgia's first fair trade organic roaster, founded here by returned Peace Corps volunteers, with a coffeehouse and a roasting operation you can watch and a sourcing model that pays the growers directly.
buzz: The roast is good and the room is where Americus meets. Ask about a roastery walk through if you are buying beans.

name: Fitzgerald Blue and Gray Museum
company: City of Fitzgerald / Fitzgerald-Ben Hill Arts Council
customer: History people, genealogy visitors, rail fans
unique: The story of a town founded in 1895 by Union veterans in the middle of the Confederacy, told inside a restored railroad depot, with Grand Army of the Republic and Confederate relics side by side in the same cases.
buzz: The founding story is the hook and most visitors have never heard it. The depot itself, with the original brick and a caboose outside, is half the visit.

name: Grand Theatre Fitzgerald
customer: Families, film people, organ enthusiasts
unique: An Art Deco house on the brick main street with one of three theatre organs still in its original building in Georgia, a 1926 Barton that gets played before films.
buzz: First run movies at small town prices in a room with a real balcony. The organ nights are the ones to catch.

name: Fitzgerald Downtown Murals and Carnegie Center
customer: Walkers, art browsers, people taking a class
unique: A Carnegie library from 1906 turned arts center, with rotating shows, an artist in residence working in the open, and murals tucked down the alleys of the surrounding historic blocks.
buzz: The murals are scattered enough to make a walk of it. The Carnegie gallery is free and the resident artist is usually happy to talk.

name: Fitzgerald Historic Downtown
customer: Architecture walkers, history travellers
unique: Brick streets and 1890s commercial blocks laid out by Union veterans on a Georgia pine ridge, with the colony's original wide avenues and a downtown that still reads as a planned northern town dropped into the south.
buzz: The street plan is the giveaway, wide and grid straight where everything around it grew organically. Easy walk with the depot and the theatre on the same blocks.
